extracted.intended_audience: patent office managers, policymakers, IP statisticians, researchers and examiners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and metrics for measuring and reporting patent office operational performance, including examination capacity, application processing times (pendency) and examination outcomes across national and regional offices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability requirements (substantive examination)
rubrics_metrics.description: The substantive examination process usually consists of determining whether the claimed innovation is novel, non-obvious and industrially applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some offices perform only formal examination (e.g., South Africa) while others undertake both formal and substantive examination (e.g., Japan). The substantive test (novelty, inventive step/non-obviousness, industrial applicability) is the core of granting decisions and affects comparisons of outcomes across offices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement and timing of request for examination
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a request for examination must be made, and the time period within which such requests must be made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedures differ: in China and Japan a request can be made up to three years after filing; in the U.S. filing implies an immediate request for examination. This affects measurement of pendency and the concept of 'potentially pending' applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fee structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Fee structure (how fees are set and applied) as a procedural dimension of office practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fee rules can influence applicant behaviour (e.g., payment deadlines, continuation filings) and therefore affect processing timelines and outcome statistics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability and procedures for accelerated examination
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether and how an applicant may request accelerated examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offices vary in the existence and mechanics of accelerated tracks; availability changes expected pendency times and comparability across offices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bilateral/multilateral work‑sharing agreements
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of work-sharing arrangements such as a patent prosecution highway (PPH).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work‑sharing can influence examination capacity and timeliness by reusing search/examination work across offices; affects cross-office comparisons of productivity and pendency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant–examiner communication process
rubrics_metrics.description: The procedures and norms governing communication between applicants (or their agents) and examiners during prosecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differences in amendment opportunities, office actions, opportunities to reply, and appeal paths can materially change pendency, outcomes and interpretation of rejection/withdrawal statistics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workload management practices (outsourcing prior art search, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: How offices manage incoming workload, for example whether the prior art search is outsourced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outsourcing, cooperation, and other workload management choices affect an office's effective examination capacity and should be considered when comparing performance metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Budget‑setting and resourcing procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: The office’s budget-setting procedure as a driver of capacity and staffing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Budget procedures determine hiring/training ability and therefore influence examiner counts, backlogs and pendency over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition and post‑grant systems
rubrics_metrics.description: The opposition system (e.g., pre‑grant, post‑grant, appeal/revocation paths).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence and form of opposition/post‑grant proceedings affect lifecycle of granted patents and how 'final' outcomes should be interpreted in cross‑office comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training, experience and incentives of patent examiners
rubrics_metrics.description: The training and experience of patent examiners, and incentives offered to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Average examiner experience affects examination quality and throughput. Annex S2 explicitly lists 'Average years of experience of examiners' as a collected statistic. Examiner incentives and composition (e.g., inclusion of hearing staff, utility model examiners) must be documented when reporting examiner counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuation/divisional and post‑rejection continuation possibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether it may be possible to continue with an application after its initial rejection by filing continuation‑in‑parts, divisional application and so on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuation and divisional mechanisms mean rejections are not final endpoints; they complicate calculation of grant rates and interpretation of rejection statistics because rejected matters can re-enter the system under new filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Potentially pending applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Potentially pending applications include all patent applications, at any stage in the process, awaiting a final decision by a patent office, including those applications for which applicants have not filed a request for examination (where applicable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The concept 'potentially pending' is preferred because in many offices the request for examination is filed after filing; using it helps cover cases where the application is at the office but examination hasn't started. Use this when assessing backlogs and stocks of work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination capacity: number of patent examiners (FTE)
rubrics_metrics.description: Number of patent examiners (full‑time equivalent, FTE), including persons conducting patent examination in affiliated institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Data on examiners should specify scope (e.g., inclusion of utility model or plant variety examiners, hearing staff). Differences in counting (headcount vs FTE) must be noted (India reported headcount). Examiner counts are the primary measure of capacity but exclude outsourced or freelance workforces unless explicitly included.

rubrics_metrics.name: Average filings per examiner
rubrics_metrics.description: Average number of patent filings per examiner for selected offices (filings per examiner).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This indicates examination capacity relative to incoming filings. Interpret cautiously: application content (claims per application, pages, complexity), outsourcing, and cooperation among offices can change the meaning of this ratio. Trend analysis at a given office is more meaningful than cross‑office raw comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pendency time (first office action and final decision)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measuring the time between the request for examination and the first office action, and between the request for examination and the final decision (or from filing where no request is required).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pendency time for first office action = average months from request for examination to first office action (or filing date where no request required). Pendency time for final decision = average months from request for examination to final decision (or filing date where no request required). Calculations can differ due to procedural differences; focus on evolution over time within an office rather than cross‑office comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant‑driven delays and their effect on pendency
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants can slow down the processing of applications at offices by amending applications, paying for extensions of time, filing requests for continued examination, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because applicants can use extensions, RCEs, amendments, and other tactics, long pendency does not necessarily imply an office is processing too slowly. Statistical interpretation must account for applicant behaviour (e.g., EPO amendments during search/exam, USPTO delays).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination outcomes breakdown
rubrics_metrics.description: Classification of examination outcomes for processed applications into: granted, rejected, withdrawn or abandoned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outcomes in a given year relate to applications filed in previous years; therefore shares of grants among processed applications should not be interpreted as grant rates on filings. Some offices rarely record 'rejection' as a final decision (e.g., Canada, Australia), so outcome distributions are not directly comparable without procedural context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on computing grant rates
rubrics_metrics.description: Challenges in calculating grant rates due to lack of data on withdrawn/abandoned/rejected before publication, processing time lags, and continuations that reintroduce rejected matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of these issues, an alternative is to focus on the outcome distribution of the applications processed by offices in a given year. Always note numerator/denominator definitions and the time lag between filing and decision when reporting grant rate statistics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annual procedural data to collect (Annex S2 list)
rubrics_metrics.description: WIPO's new questionnaire collected: (A) Number of patent examination decisions in the given year broken down by granted, rejected, withdrawn/abandoned; (B) Number of patent examiners (FTE); (C) Average years of experience of examiners; (D) Average time (months) from request for examination to first office action; (E) Average time (months) from request for examination to final decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These five items form a core set of comparable procedural indicators. When reporting, include notes on definitions, scope, and any office‑specific caveats (e.g., inclusion of utility model examiners, how 'final decision' is defined).

rubrics_metrics.name: Data caveats and office‑specific notes
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedural differences and office‑specific recording practices limit cross‑country comparison; e.g., Canada treats abandoned files as suspended rather than rejected; EPO first action data include searches done for national offices; Japan and Korea include utility model examiners; U.S. includes plant variety applications in examiner counts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comparing offices or publishing statistics, explicitly document such country notes. Prefer trend analysis for a given office rather than raw cross‑office comparisons unless offices have similar procedures and definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended interpretation principle: focus on trends within an office
rubrics_metrics.description: To address data limitations and procedural heterogeneity, it is more meaningful to focus on trends at a given office rather than direct cross‑office comparisons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use longitudinal analysis to assess changes in capacity, pendency and outcomes. Where cross‑office comparisons are made, restrict to offices with similar procedures or explicitly adjust/annotate differences.
